# How a change goes from intent to production

A change lives in `changes/<name>/`. The business writes `intent.md` there.
Each phase is done by a fresh session that reads the artifacts of the
earlier phases and leaves its own for the next one. The files are the only
memory, so write each artifact for a reader who was not there. Below,
`<change>` stands for `changes/<name>/`.

| # | Phase | Reads | Leaves |
|---|-------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Spec | `<change>/intent.md`, the code, `docs/` | `<change>/spec.md` |
| 2 | Plan | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `<change>/plan.md` |
| 3 | Implement | `<change>/plan.md`, `<change>/spec.md` | code, `docs/architecture.md` |
| - | Preview (a person) | `## For the preview` in `plan.md` | `<change>/preview.md` |
| 4 | Unit tests | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/` |
| 5 | System test | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/system/`, `<change>/test-report.md` |
| 6 | Lint | the code | clean ruff |
| 7 | Code review | everything | `<change>/review.md` |
| 8 | Review fixes | `<change>/review.md` | fixes, ticked `review.md` |
| 9 | Deploy | `docs/deploy.md` | a release in production |

## 1. Spec

Turn the intent into `spec.md`, the design an engineer builds from. No
code. Start from how the system works today (`docs/architecture.md` and the
code) and describe the change against it: the new and changed rules; the
API changes, with request and response examples and every new error; how
the server enforces the rules without keeping state; the page (what shows
when, keyboard and screen-reader use, small screens); which modules change
and how; what must keep working exactly as before; and how each line of the
intent's "How we will know it worked" and "What must not change" will be
checked. End with **Open questions**: each one gets the decision you took,
so nothing blocks the next phase.

## 2. Plan

Turn `spec.md` into `plan.md`, an implementation plan. No code. The first
line is `# Plan: <title>`. Then 2 to 4 phases, each a heading
`## Phase N: <name>` followed only by task lines `- [ ] <task>`, 3 to 6
tasks each. Each phase ends with a task that verifies it by running
something, and leaves the game working. Verification uses what every
session has: `python3` (the tests, a throwaway script, a server started
with `--port 0` and driven with `urllib`) and `ruff`. No browser and no
other tools: how the page looks and feels is checked by a person at the
preview after phase 3, so list those checks under a final heading
`## For the preview` as plain bullets, not boxes. Writing new tests is
phase 4 of this process, not part of this plan, but the existing tests
must keep passing after every phase.

## 3. Implement

Implement the first phase of `plan.md` that still has unchecked boxes, and
only that phase. Tick each box (`- [ ]` to `- [x]`) as soon as its task is
done, one edit per task. Follow `spec.md`. If you must depart from it,
update `spec.md` so the two agree. Keep `docs/architecture.md` true. Do not
write new tests yet, but run the existing ones. If a verify task asks for
something you cannot run, do the part you can, tick it, and add what is
left to `## For the preview`.

## Preview (done by a person)

A person runs the change on a preview server, goes through
`## For the preview`, and records the result in `preview.md`: who, when,
and what passed or failed. That file is the sign-off for everything only a
browser can show. Later phases read it; they do not repeat those checks.

## 4. Unit tests

Write pytest tests in `tests/` for every rule in `spec.md`, next to the
existing ones: every new rule, every new error, and every "must not change"
promise of the intent. Call the code directly, not over the network. Run
the whole suite. If a test finds a bug, fix the code and say so in your
final message.

## 5. System test

Test the real system from the outside, extending `tests/system/`: start
`python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a process and, over HTTP, play the new
feature end to end, including the attempts the intent says must fail, and
show that the old game still behaves as before. Always stop the server,
even when a test fails. Run the whole suite. Write `test-report.md`: what
was tested, the result, and any bugs found and fixed.

## 6. Lint

Run `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`. Fix every finding in the
code, run the tests again, and stop when both are clean and the tests pass.
Never silence a finding (see `CLAUDE.md`).

## 7. Code review

Act as a reviewer who did not write this change. Read the intent, the spec,
the diff of the change (`git diff` against the commit before its spec) and
the code around it. Look for: bugs; gaps between intent, spec, code and
`docs/architecture.md`; rules that are not tested; security (the server
faces the internet and trusts no request); and accessibility. The browser
checks belong to `preview.md`: a problem it reports is a finding, but how
much a sign-off is worth (who looked, how closely) is for whoever releases
to judge, so say it in the verdict, not as a finding. Do not change any
code. Write `review.md`: one line per finding,

```markdown
- [ ] **blocker|major|minor** `path:line`: what is wrong, and why it matters
```

most severe first, then a one-paragraph verdict. If there is nothing to
report at some severity, say so; do not invent findings.

## 8. Review fixes

Fix every blocker and major finding in `review.md`, and the minors that
are cheap. Tick each finding as you fix it. Leave a finding you decide not
to fix unticked, with the reason after it. Add a test for every bug you
fix. Finish with the tests and lint clean.

## 9. Deploy

Follow `docs/deploy.md`.

# Plan: a secret cheat code (`cheat-code`)

## Phase 1: The rules and the signing key (no change to the API yet)

- [x] `tictactoe/game.py`: add a keyword `steals=0` to `turn`, `validate` and
  `play`, following spec rule 4. X is to move when X count − O count ==
  `steals`, and a valid board has X − O equal to `steals` or `steals + 1`.
  With `steals=0`, every result, error message and the order of the checks
  stay exactly as they are today. `outcome()` and `legal_moves()` do not
  change.
- [x] `tictactoe/game.py`: add `steal(board, cell, steals) -> list[str]`. It
  raises `IllegalMoveError` with the spec's exact messages, in the spec's
  order: `steals` already 1 ("you have already stolen a square in this
  game"), `cell` not a whole number 0–8 with `bool` refused ("steal must be a
  whole number from 0 to 8"), game over ("the game is over"), not X's turn
  under `steals` ("against the computer you play X"), cell not an `"O"`
  ("you can only steal one of the computer's squares"). It returns a new
  board with that cell set to `"X"` and never changes its input.
- [x] `tictactoe/ai.py`: add a keyword `steals=0` to
  `choose_move(board, level, rng=None, *, steals=0)` and an argument to
  `best_move` and `value`, so the `@cache` key includes it. Pass it to every
  `game.turn`, `game.play` and recursive call, including Easy's check for a
  winning move. With `steals=0` the moves must be exactly today's.
- [x] New `tictactoe/signing.py`, as the spec's "Game token" section
  describes. The key is `TICTACTOE_SECRET` encoded as UTF-8 when it is set
  and not empty, otherwise `secrets.token_bytes(32)`, made once at import.
  This is the only module that reads `os.environ`. `sign(board, level,
  steals)` returns `"<s>.<64 lowercase hex>"`: the HMAC-SHA256 of
  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with each cell written as `X`,
  `O` or `-`. `verify(token, board, level) -> int` returns `s`. It raises
  `IllegalMoveError("the game token does not match this game")` when the
  token is not a `str`, does not have exactly the shape `0.`/`1.` followed
  by 64 lowercase hex digits, or has a MAC that does not match. It compares
  with `hmac.compare_digest`. The key never appears in a return value, an
  error or a log.
- [x] `docs/architecture.md`, Modules table: describe the turn rule with
  `steals`, `game.steal`, `ai`'s `steals` argument and the new `signing.py`.
- [x] Verify: `python3 -m pytest -q` passes with no test changed, and
  `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` are clean. Then run a throwaway
  `python3` script, kept outside `tests/`. (a) It gets the committed code of
  commit `74dcd2d` with `git show 74dcd2d:tictactoe/<file>` into a temporary
  package. For every position reachable by legal play from the empty board,
  it checks that the new `turn`, `validate`, `play` and Hard
  `choose_move(..., steals=0)` match the old ones. It also checks that a set
  of impossible boards gets the same error message from both. (b) On the
  spec's board `X O _ / _ O _ / _ _ X`: `steal(…, 4, 0)` wins on the diagonal
  0-4-8. `steal(…, 1, 0)` gives `turn(…, steals=1) == "O"`, and Hard
  `choose_move(…, steals=1)` answers 2. Each `steal` error from task 2 has
  its exact message, and the input board is unchanged. (c) For
  `sign`/`verify`: a round trip returns `s`. A different board, a different
  level, a flipped `0.`/`1.` prefix, one changed hex digit, an uppercase MAC,
  a non-string and an empty string are all rejected. With
  `TICTACTOE_SECRET=abc` set, two separate processes make the same token.
  Without it, two processes make different tokens.

## Phase 2: The move API judges steals

- [x] `tictactoe/server.py` `handle_move`: read the optional `game` and
  `steal`. A request with neither must go through exactly today's checks in
  today's order, with `steals=0`. A request that has either one is checked
  in this order. First, today's checks of the body, the board's shape, the
  mode and the level. Then the token, when `game` is present (verify it
  against `board` and `level`, which gives `s`). Then "send either cell or
  steal, not both", "you can only steal from the computer" (friend mode),
  "a steal needs the game token from the last answer", and last
  `game.validate(board, steals=s)` with the X-to-move check under `s`. After
  that come `game.steal`'s own errors, or `game.play`'s errors for a normal
  move. Keep the signature `handle_move(request)`.
- [x] `handle_move`: play the steal (`game.steal`, after which `s` becomes 1)
  or the move (`game.play(..., steals=s)`). If the game goes on in computer
  mode, play the computer's reply with
  `ai.choose_move(board, level, steals=s)`. Pass `steals` to
  `describe(board, steals)` so that `turn` is right after a steal.
- [x] Add the four new answer fields to every `200` answer, in every mode.
  `game`: a new token only in computer mode while `playing`. It keeps the
  request token's `s` (or 1 after the steal), or has `s = 0` when there was
  no token and the request's board was empty. Otherwise it is `null`.
  `stealable`: the O cells when the new token has `s = 0`, the game is
  `playing` and X is to move, otherwise `[]`. `steal_used`: `s == 1`.
  `assisted`: `won` and `winner == "X"` and `steal_used`. Tokenless answers
  keep every old field with the same value. In `Handler.do_POST`, after a
  successful steal, write one line through `self.log_message`:
  `steal level=<level> cell=<n> status=<status> assisted=<true|false>`, and
  log nothing else: no token, no key, no board.
- [x] `docs/architecture.md`, "The move API": add `steal` and `game` to the
  request, add `game`, `stealable`, `steal_used` and `assisted` to the
  answer, and describe the game token and why the server can stay stateless
  with it, the turn rule after a steal, every new error and the steal log
  line.
- [x] Verify: `python3 -m pytest -q` passes with no test changed, and ruff
  is clean. Then run a throwaway `python3` script that calls `handle_move`
  directly. It plays the spec's examples, sending each answer's `game` back
  with the next request: first move, second move, steal 4 (an assisted win
  with `game` `null`), and steal 1 from the same position (computer replies
  2, token starts with `1.`, `stealable == []`). A second steal with the
  `1.` token gets 400 "already stolen". Every new error in the spec's table
  gets its exact message, including the order when two errors apply at
  once. Friend-mode answers have the four fields with their empty values, a
  tokenless mid-game board gets `game: null`, and steals work at Easy too.
  For every reachable X-to-move board (Hard and friend mode) and for the
  bad requests in `tests/test_server.py`, the answer without its four new
  keys (or the error) equals what the code of commit `74dcd2d` answers
  (loaded with `git show` as in Phase 1).
- [x] Verify the real server: start `python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a
  process, with stdout and stderr captured, read the URL from its first
  line, and drive it with `urllib`. `/health` answers `200 ok`. A whole
  game against Hard steals and wins with `assisted: true`, and a second
  steal from a kept token answers 400. A whole tokenless game against Hard
  ends without an X win. Stop the server in a `finally`, then check that
  stderr holds exactly one `steal level=hard …` line per successful steal
  and never contains a token's hex. Start two servers one after the other
  with the same `TICTACTOE_SECRET`: a token from the first is accepted by
  the second.

## Phase 3: The page carries the token (nothing visible changes)

- [ ] `tictactoe/static/app.js`: `newGame()` starts with `game: null`,
  `stealable: []`, `steal_used: false` and `assisted: false` in `state`.
  Every move request sends `game: state.game` (or leaves it out when it is
  `null`). Errors (for example after a development restart: "the game token
  does not match this game") show in the status line as today, and New game
  recovers.
- [ ] `tictactoe/static/index.html`: add the cheat panel under the status
  line, with `hidden`: a `<button type="button">` "Steal a square" with
  `aria-pressed="false"` and a text paragraph, each with an `id` for
  `app.js`. Add a fourth score column ("With help", `id="score-help"`),
  whose `th` and `td` are both `hidden`. Change no other label or text.
- [ ] `tictactoe/static/style.css`: a `.cell.stealable` dashed outline that
  does not rely on colour alone and is visible in light and dark mode, the
  panel's layout, a steal button at least 44 px tall, and a four-column
  score table that fits 320 px wide with no horizontal scroll. Hidden
  elements stay hidden, so the page looks exactly as it does today.
- [ ] Verify: `python3 -m pytest -q` passes, and ruff is clean. Start
  `python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` and, with `urllib`, check that `/`,
  `/static/app.js` and `/static/style.css` answer 200 and that in the HTML
  the panel and both "With help" cells carry `hidden`. Then replay the
  requests `app.js` now sends (an empty board without `game`, then each
  answer's `game` sent back) through whole games against Easy and Hard and
  in friend mode: every answer is 200 and the games end normally. Stop the
  server in a `finally`.

## Phase 4: The cheat on the page

- [ ] `app.js`, the code: a `keydown` listener on `document` keeps the last
  10 keys and compares them with
  `ArrowUp ArrowUp ArrowDown ArrowDown ArrowLeft ArrowRight ArrowLeft ArrowRight b a`,
  with B and A in either case. It ignores events with Ctrl, Alt or Meta
  held, `event.repeat`, and keys typed while a `<select>` has the focus. It
  unlocks only when the mode is `computer` and `state.status` is
  `playing`, and otherwise does nothing at all. New game, a mode change or a
  level change locks it again and clears the keys. On unlock, the status
  line says "Cheat unlocked! Once this game, you may steal one of the
  computer's squares." The board's own arrow handling does not change.
- [ ] `app.js`, the panel: unlocking shows the panel and the "With help"
  column. The column stays visible until the page is reloaded. The button is
  `aria-disabled="true"` (still focusable) when `state.stealable` is empty.
  The panel text is then "No O to steal yet" when `steal_used` is false, or
  "Steal used" when it is true. Otherwise it is "Press Steal, then choose an
  O. Esc cancels."
- [ ] `app.js`, steal mode: the button (click, Enter, Space) turns steal
  mode on only when `stealable` is not empty. It sets `aria-pressed`, says
  "Steal: choose one of the computer's squares." and moves the focus to the
  lowest stealable square, using the roving `tabindex`. In steal mode, only
  the squares in `state.stealable` are `aria-disabled="false"` with class
  `stealable` and the label suffix ", can be stolen". Choosing one sends
  `{board, steal, mode, level, game}`. Steal mode ends when the answer
  arrives, or with Esc or a second press of the button, which puts the
  focus back on the button. Outside steal mode, an O does nothing, as
  today.
- [ ] `app.js`, after a steal: the status line says "You stole row R,
  column C." when the game goes on, and the usual text comes back on the
  next render. A win with `assisted: true` shows "You won... with a little
  help", adds 1 to "With help" and adds nothing to X wins. O wins and draws
  count as today. `app.js` uses `stealable`, `steal_used` and `assisted`
  exactly as the server sends them, and never works out a rule itself.
- [ ] `docs/architecture.md`, "The page": the code and how the page
  recognises it, locking per game, the panel, steal mode and its keyboard
  and screen-reader behaviour, and the "With help" score.

# Spec: a secret cheat code (`cheat-code`)

Source: `changes/cheat-code/intent.md`. This is the design to build from.
It describes the change against the system as it is today
(`docs/architecture.md`, `tictactoe/`).

## Summary

Against the computer, typing ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A on the page unlocks a
**steal** for the current game: once per game the player may turn one of
the computer's O squares into an X, and that is the player's move. A win
that used a steal is announced as "You won... with a little help" and
counted in its own score column, never as a normal win.

The browser recognises the code and shows the steal controls. The server
judges every steal. To enforce "one steal per game" without keeping state,
the server signs each game position it hands out (an HMAC **game token**)
and accepts a steal only together with a valid token that says no steal has
been used. Requests without a token behave exactly as today.

## How it works today (the parts this change touches)

- A board is 9 cells, `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. Whose turn it is follows from
  the counts: `game.turn()` is X when X count == O count. `game.validate()`
  accepts a board only if X count − O count is 0 or 1.
- `POST /api/move` takes the whole board, `cell`, `mode`, `level`. Against
  the computer the player is X and the board must have X to move. The server
  plays `cell`, then the computer's reply, and answers the new board.
- The server trusts nothing: any board that passes `validate()` is accepted.
  It has no idea whether that board came from a real game.
- The score (X wins, O wins, draws) lives in `app.js` until reload.

## New and changed rules

1. **Steal.** In a game against the computer, on the player's turn (X to
   move, game still playing), the player may name one cell that holds `"O"`.
   That cell becomes `"X"`. This is the player's move: the computer then
   replies as usual if the game goes on.
2. **Once per game.** A game has at most one steal. A game is one unbroken
   chain of positions handed out by the server, starting from the empty
   board (see "Game token").
3. **Only against the computer**, at both levels (`easy`, `hard`). Never in
   `friend` mode.
4. **Turn after a steal.** A steal changes a mark without adding one, so the
   counts no longer say whose turn it is. The rule becomes: with `s` steals
   used in the game (0 or 1), X is to move when X count − O count == `s`,
   otherwise O. A valid board has X count − O count equal to `s` or `s + 1`.
   With `s = 0` both rules are exactly today's.
5. **A steal can win at once.** If the stolen square completes a line of X,
   the game is won by X and the computer does not move. A steal never fills
   an empty square, so it cannot cause a draw by itself.
6. **Assisted win.** A game won by X in which a steal was used is an
   *assisted* win. The server says so in every answer (`assisted: true`).
   The page announces it as "You won... with a little help" and counts it
   only in the "With help" column, not in "X wins".
7. After a steal the game goes on normally: the computer (either level)
   plays its best/random move from the new position, and the computer can
   still win or draw. Those are counted as today (O win, draw).
8. **The code.** ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A (`ArrowUp ArrowUp ArrowDown ArrowDown
   ArrowLeft ArrowRight ArrowLeft ArrowRight b a`, B and A in either case).
   The code is recognised by the page only; it unlocks the steal controls
   for the current game. The server does not check the code (see Open
   questions 1).

## Game token (how the server enforces the rules without state)

The server keeps nothing between requests. Instead it signs what it must
trust when the browser sends it back, as `CLAUDE.md` allows.

- **Key.** `TICTACTOE_SECRET` from the environment (UTF-8 bytes) when set
  and not empty; otherwise 32 random bytes from `secrets.token_bytes` made
  once when the process starts. Production sets it through `ops/deploy.sh`
  and keeps it across releases, so tokens survive a deploy. The key is
  never logged, never sent, never put in an error message.
- **Format.** `"<s>.<mac>"`, where `<s>` is the number of steals used (`0`
  or `1`) and `<mac>` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the message
  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with `<cells>` the 9 cells, each
  written as `X`, `O` or `-`. Example: `"0.3f9a…c1"` (64 hex digits).
  The token binds the board, the level and the steal count together;
  change any of them and it no longer verifies.
- **Checking.** Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`. A token that is not a
  string, has the wrong shape, an `<s>` other than `0`/`1`, or a MAC that
  does not match the request's `board` and `level` is rejected with
  `400 {"error": "the game token does not match this game"}`. This applies
  to any request that carries a `game` field, steal or not.
- **When the server hands one out** (the `game` field of the answer), only
  in `computer` mode and only while the game is still `playing`:
  - the request carried a valid token: the new position gets a token with
    the same `s` (or `s = 1` if this request was the steal);
  - the request had no token and its board was empty (first move of a new
    game): the new position gets a token with `s = 0`;
  - otherwise (no token, board not empty, e.g. a hand-made mid-game board

address):

```text

```

Nothing else is logged: no token, no key, no board. Because a steal needs a
token chain that started from an empty board, every logged steal happened
in a real game played through the server.

## The page

### Before the code (unchanged)

The page looks and behaves exactly as today: no steal button, no hint, no
"With help" column, no change to labels or status texts. The new elements
exist in `index.html` with `hidden` and are not shown or announced.

### Recognising the code

- `app.js` listens to `keydown` on `document` and keeps the last 10 keys.
  When they equal the code, the code is typed. A sliding window means extra
  keys before it do not matter (↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ … still works).
- Ignored: events with Ctrl, Alt or Meta held, and auto-repeat
  (`event.repeat`). Keys typed while focus is in a `<select>` are not
  recorded (arrows there change the mode or level, which starts a new game).
- The board's own arrow handling stays as it is: typing the code with the
  focus on the board moves the focus around, which is harmless; arrows never
  play a move.
- The code unlocks only when the mode is `computer` and the game is
  `playing`. Otherwise it does nothing at all (friend mode: no message, no
  hint).
- Unlocking lasts for the current game. A new game (button, mode or level
  change) locks it again; typing the code again unlocks it again.

### After the code

- The status line (`aria-live`) announces: "Cheat unlocked! Once this game,
  you may steal one of the computer's squares." The current status text
  follows after the next move as usual.
- A panel under the status line appears with a **Steal a square** button
  (`aria-pressed`) and the short text "Press Steal, then choose an O. Esc
  cancels." The button is disabled-looking (`aria-disabled="true"`, still
  focusable) when `stealable` is empty, with the reason in the panel text:
  "No O to steal yet" before the computer has moved, "Steal used" after.
- The score table shows a fourth column **With help** (and keeps showing it
  until the page is reloaded, so the count stays visible).

### Steal mode

- Pressing the button (click, Enter, Space) turns steal mode on, but only
  if `stealable` is not empty. The status line says "Steal: choose one of
  the computer's squares." The focus moves to the lowest stealable square
  (roving `tabindex` as today).
- In steal mode only the squares in `stealable` are active
  (`aria-disabled="false"`, class `stealable` with a visible dashed outline
  that does not rely on colour alone). Their label gains ", can be stolen",
  e.g. "Row 2, column 2, O, can be stolen". Every other square is
  `aria-disabled="true"` and does nothing when chosen.
- Choosing a stealable square (click, tap, Enter, Space) sends
  `{board, steal, mode, level, game}`. Steal mode ends with the answer.
- Esc, or pressing the button again, ends steal mode without a move and
  puts the focus back on the button.
- Outside steal mode, clicking an O does nothing, as today.

### After a steal

- The status line says "You stole row R, column C." when the game goes on
  (then the usual "Your turn (X)" on the next render), and "You won... with
  a little help" when the steal or a later move wins with `assisted: true`.
- Score: `assisted: true` adds 1 to **With help** and nothing to X wins.
  A computer win or a draw after a steal counts as today.
- The panel says "Steal used" and the button stays disabled-looking.

### Small screens

The panel and the four-column score table must fit 320 px wide with no
horizontal scroll: the column headings are short ("X wins", "O wins",
"Draws", "With help") and the button is at least 44 px tall. The code
needs a keyboard, so phones without one cannot unlock it (Open questions 2).

| File | Change |

  (`test_hard_never_loses` passes untouched). Easy is unchanged.

  1024-byte limit, the keyboard model of the board and its labels.

| Intent line | Check |
|-------------|-------|
| Code unlocks one steal for that game; computer's mark becomes the player's; counts as the move | Unit (`game.steal`, `handle_move`) and system test: play a game over HTTP with tokens, steal, see the cell become X and the computer reply. | One steal per game | Unit and system: a second steal with the returned token → 400 "already stolen". |
| Never shown or hinted at until the code; then clear how to use it | Preview: page before the code is identical to today (no button, no column, no label change); after the code the panel, text and announcement appear. |
| The code is ↑↑↓↓←→←→BA | Preview: the exact code unlocks; a wrong key in the middle does not; the sliding window works; uppercase B A works. |

## Open questions (with the decision taken)

1. **Should the server check the code?** No. The code is meant to be
   shared, so anyone sending requests by hand knows it anyway; making the
   browser send it would add nothing. "Nobody can steal without the code"
   is a promise about the page, kept by the page. The server enforces what
   it can: computer mode only, a real game, at most one steal.
2. **Phones and tablets without a keyboard?** Out of scope: the intent says
   "typed on the keyboard". No touch gesture is added. Product can ask for
   one as a separate change.
3. **Replaying an older token to steal in a different branch of the same
   game?** Allowed: it cannot be stopped without server state, and each
   branch still has at most one steal. Equivalent to starting over and
   replaying the same moves.
4. **Tokens for games already running when this ships?** Those pages run
   the old `app.js` and never send `game`; they play on as today and cannot
   steal. After a reload they get tokens.
5. **Development restarts.** Without `TICTACTOE_SECRET`, a restart makes a
   new key, so a game in progress gets 400 "the game token does not match"
   on its next move. Accepted for development; the page shows its usual
   error and New game fixes it. Production keeps its key across releases.
6. **Is an assisted win also an X win in the API?** Yes: `status: "won"`,
   `winner: "X"` as today, plus `assisted: true`. Only the page's score
   counts it separately. Keeps old clients and `status` unchanged.
7. **Can the computer still win after a steal?** Yes, and that is counted
   as a normal O win; a draw after a steal is a normal draw. Only X wins
   are "with help".
8. **Token after the game ends?** `null`: there is nothing left to play.
9. **Where the code lives in `app.js`.** Plain in the source. It is a
   shared secret by design; hiding it would be theatre.

# Architecture

```text
browser (static/)                          server (Python, stdlib)
┌───────────────────────┐  POST /api/move  ┌────────────────────────────┐
│ index.html  app.js    │ ───────────────▶ │ server.py  handle_move()   │
│ draws, sends clicks,  │    whole board   │   ├─ game.py  rules        │
│ keeps the score       │ ◀─────────────── │   └─ ai.py    computer     │
└───────────────────────┘   new board +    └────────────────────────────┘
                            outcome
```

The rules live in Python only. The browser never decides whether a move is
legal or who won: it shows what the server answers.

## Modules (`tictactoe/`)

| File | Job |
|------|-----|
| `game.py` | The rules. A board is a list of 9 cells, row by row, each `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. X moves first, so `turn(board, steals=0)` follows from the counts: with `steals` steals used in the game (0 or 1), X is to move when X count − O count == `steals`. `check_cells(board)` checks only a board's shape and cells, `validate(board, steals=0)` checks a whole board from outside (`check_cells`, then X − O must be `steals` or `steals + 1`), `play(board, cell, steals=0)` returns a new board (never changes its input) or raises `IllegalMoveError`, `steal(board, cell, steals)` returns a new board with the O on `cell` turned into an X (once per game, on X's turn, only an O), `outcome()` says `playing`, `won` (with winner and line) or `draw`. With `steals=0` everything is the plain game. |
| `ai.py` | The computer. `choose_move(board, level, rng=None, *, steals=0)`: **hard** is negamax over the full game tree, cached (per board and `steals`), lowest cell among equals, so it is deterministic and never loses; **easy** takes a winning move if it sees one, otherwise plays at random. `steals` is passed on to every rule call, so the search knows whose turn it is after a steal. |
| `signing.py` | The game token. The key is `TICTACTOE_SECRET` when set and not empty, otherwise 32 random bytes made at start-up; it is the only module that reads `os.environ`, and the key never leaves it. `sign(board, level, steals)` returns `"<s>.<mac>"`, the HMAC-SHA256 (lowercase hex) of `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, cells written `X`, `O` or `-`. `verify(token, board, level)` returns `s`, or raises `IllegalMoveError("the game token does not match this game")`; it compares with `hmac.compare_digest`. |
| `server.py` | `ThreadingHTTPServer`. Serves a fixed map of assets (no request path reaches the file system), `/health`, and the move API (`handle_move`, with `check_steal_request` for requests that carry a token or a steal). Keeps no state: what it must trust it signs with `signing.py`. Logs one line per successful steal. |
| `__main__.py` | `python3 -m tictactoe [--host] [--port]`; prints the URL it listens on. |
| `static/` | `index.html`, `style.css`, `app.js`. No build step, no libraries. |

## The move API

`POST /api/move`, a JSON body of at most 1024 bytes:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 2, "mode": "computer", "level": "hard",
 "game": "0.<64 hex>"}
```

- `mode` is `computer` (default) or `friend`; `level` is `easy` or `hard`
  (default), used only against the computer.
- Against the computer the player is always X, so the board must have X
  to move.
- The server plays `cell` for whoever is to move, then, against the
  computer and if the game goes on, the computer's reply as O.
- `game` (optional) is the token from the previous answer. `steal`
  (optional, instead of `cell`) is a cell holding an O that the player
  turns into an X, as their move: once per game, only against the computer,
  and only together with a `game` token. A field sent as `null` counts as
  not sent.

Answer `200`:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "X", "", "O", "", "", "", "O"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 8,
 "game": "0.<64 hex>", "stealable": [4, 8], "steal_used": false, "assisted": false}
```

`status` is `playing`, `won` or `draw`; `line` is the three winning cells;
`turn` is `null` once the game is over; `computer_move` is `null` when the
computer did not move. `game` is the token for the new position (below) or
`null`; `stealable` lists the O cells when the answer's token has `s = 0`,
the game is playing and X is to move, else `[]`; `steal_used` is `true`
once the game has used its steal; `assisted` is `true` for a win by X with
`steal_used`. The page uses these as given and works out none of them.

### The game token, and why the server stays stateless

To allow one steal per game without remembering games, the server signs
each position it hands out (`signing.py`): the token `"<s>.<mac>"` binds
the board, the level and `s`, the steals used so far. It is handed out
only in `computer` mode while the game is `playing`: with the request's
`s` (or `1` after a steal) when the request carried a valid token, with
`s = 0` when the request had no token and an empty board (a new game), and
otherwise `game` is `null` (a hand-made mid-game board plays as before but
can never steal). A steal needs an `s = 0` token; after it every token in
that game has `s = 1`, and forging one needs the key. An old token stays
valid, so a player can go back to an earlier position of the same game
and steal there: a branch, which still has at most one steal.

**Turn after a steal.** A steal changes a mark without adding one, so with
`s` steals used X is to move when X − O == `s`, and a valid board has
X − O equal to `s` or `s + 1`. With `s = 0` this is the plain rule.

**Without `game` and `steal`** a request goes through exactly the old
checks and gets the old answer, plus the four new fields.

Errors: `400 {"error": "..."}` for any bad input (bad JSON, impossible
board, taken square, game over, unknown mode or level), `411` without a
`Content-Length`, `413` for a body over 1024 bytes, `404` for other paths,
`405` for `GET /api/move`. A request with `game` or `steal` is checked in
this order: the body, the board's shape and cells, mode, level; then

| Case | Message |
|------|---------|
| `game` does not verify for this `board` and `level` | `the game token does not match this game` |
| both `cell` and `steal` | `send either cell or steal, not both` |
| `steal` in `friend` mode | `you can only steal from the computer` |
| `steal` without `game` | `a steal needs the game token from the last answer` |
| X − O outside `s`..`s + 1` | `X moves first and the players alternate` |
| not X to move under `s`, against the computer | `against the computer you play X` |
| `steal` with an `s = 1` token | `you have already stolen a square in this game` |
| `steal` not a whole number 0–8 | `steal must be a whole number from 0 to 8` |
| the game is over | `the game is over` |
| the cell is not an O | `you can only steal one of the computer's squares` |

A normal move with a token then gets `play`'s usual errors.

**Log.** After each successful steal the server writes one line through
`log_message` (stderr), `steal level=hard cell=4 status=won assisted=true`,
and nothing else: no token, no key, no board.

## The page

`app.js` holds the current answer from the server and the score (X wins, O
wins, draws, until the page is reloaded). Each click or Enter/Space on a
square sends one move. The board is one tab stop: arrow keys, Home and End
move between squares (roving `tabindex`), and every square has an
`aria-label` such as "Row 1, column 3, X, winning". The status line is an
`aria-live` region. Changing mode or level starts a new game.

## Tests

- `tests/test_game.py`, `tests/test_ai.py`, `tests/test_server.py`: unit

  as X and as O.
- `tests/system/test_http.py`: starts `python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a
  process and tests it over HTTP: health, assets, 404s, whole games, errors.
